items.question: In the cache-aside pattern, what does an application do on a cache hit and on a cache miss, and how does this differ from read-through caching?

accepted.quote: A cache-aside sequence reads the cache first, fetches the origin on a miss
accepted.rationale: Cache-first read; a miss fetches the origin, and the same section's flow returns the cached value on a hit.

accepted.quote: A read-through cache loads a miss from the source on behalf of the caller
accepted.rationale: Read-through performs the fill in the cache, unlike application-owned cache-aside fill.

items.answer_key: The application reads the cache first; a hit returns the cached item directly. On a miss it loads the item from the data store, writes it into the cache, and returns it to the caller. Read-through caching differs because the cache itself performs the load on a miss, while cache-aside keeps that logic in the application.
key_facts: The application checks the cache before going to the data store.
On a miss the application reads from the data store, populates the cache, and returns the value.
Read-through caching performs the load inside the caching system; cache-aside emulates it in application code.
Only data that is actually requested is loaded into the cache.

items.question: A service handles a long-run average of 250 requests per second, and each request spends an average of 120 ms in the system. Using Little's law, what is the average number of requests in the system, and what condition must hold for the law to apply?

accepted.quote: For a stable system with a consistent customer/work definition and well-defined steady-state
accepted.rationale: States the stable/steady-state precondition; the same section gives the mean identity.
Applying the identity to 250 requests/s and 0.12 s gives 30 average requests.

items.answer_key: Convert the dwell time to seconds and multiply: L = 250 x 0.12 = 30 requests on average. The law is an average-case identity for a stationary (ergodic) system; apart from that, it does not depend on the arrival distribution, the service-time distribution or the queue discipline.
key_facts: L = lambda x W relates average items in the system, average arrival rate and average time in the system.
With lambda = 250/s and W = 0.12 s, L = 30.
The result is a long-run average that requires an ergodic, stationary system.
The identity applies to whole systems and to subsystems within them.

items.question: A five-server Raft cluster uses majority quorums. How many server failures can it tolerate while still electing a leader and committing new entries, and what property of majorities keeps two partitions from both making progress?

accepted.rationale: A majority of five is three, so two failures are tolerable.

accepted.quote: a minority partition cannot commit authoritatively
accepted.rationale: Intersecting majorities leave only the majority side able to commit.

items.answer_key: Five servers require a majority of three, so the cluster can lose two servers and still elect a leader and commit entries; with three failures only two remain, below quorum. Quorums are counted over all configured servers rather than only the reachable ones, and any two majorities share at least one server. That shared server can vote in only one term and can sit on only one side of a partition, so at most one partition can assemble a quorum and split brain is avoided.
key_facts: A majority of five servers is three, so two failures are tolerable.
Majorities are computed over the full configured membership, not the live set.
Any two majority quorums intersect in at least one server.
At most one partition of a split network can hold a majority.

items.question: Under RFC 9110, which request methods are idempotent, and when may a client automatically retry a request whose method is not idempotent?

accepted.quote: PUT, DELETE and safe methods are idempotent by their specified semantics.
accepted.rationale: States the RFC 9110 method-level idempotence set.

accepted.quote: POST has no general automatic-retry guarantee.
accepted.rationale: Non-idempotent methods are not automatically retryable.

accepted.quote: semantically idempotent, or protected by an application effect key
accepted.rationale: States the corpus retry precondition: idempotent semantics or an application effect key.

items.answer_key: RFC 9110 defines idempotence in terms of the intended effect on the server: several identical requests must have the same effect as one. PUT, DELETE, and every safe method (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, and TRACE) are idempotent. A client should not automatically retry a non-idempotent request unless it knows the request semantics are actually idempotent or can detect that the original request was never applied; a proxy must not automatically retry non-idempotent requests at all.
key_facts: Idempotence concerns the intended effect on server state, not incidental effects such as access logging.
RFC 9110 counts PUT, DELETE, GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, and TRACE as idempotent; POST and PATCH are not guaranteed to be idempotent.
Automatic retries of non-idempotent methods require knowledge of idempotent semantics or evidence that the original request was not applied.
A proxy must not automatically retry non-idempotent requests, and a client should not automatically retry a failed automatic retry.

items.question: What distinguishes head-based from tail-based trace sampling, and why can head sampling alone fail to retain every trace that contains an error?

accepted.quote: | Head sampling | Can limit collection near request start | Later severe error may be missed |
accepted.rationale: Head sampling decides near request start, so a later error can be missed.

accepted.quote: | Tail sampling | Can prefer slow/error traces using fuller context | Requires buffered state and collector resources; decisions can be late |
accepted.rationale: Tail sampling uses fuller context but needs buffering; the contrast explains the distinction.

items.answer_key: Head sampling decides early, often from the trace ID and a target percentage, without inspecting the finished trace; this keeps whole traces at a consistent rate but cannot condition on errors or total latency. Tail sampling waits until all or most spans are available and can sample by error presence, overall latency, span attributes, or attributes that identify a newly deployed service. That is why a team wanting every error trace may need tail sampling, possibly after an initial head-sampling stage.
key_facts: Head sampling makes an early decision without inspecting the whole trace.
Consistent probability sampling by trace ID retains whole traces at a fixed rate.
Tail sampling decides after all or most spans are available.
Tail criteria can include errors, total latency, span attributes, and attributes that identify a newly deployed service.
